title: Playing with Fire, Losing the Drive: Bidirectional Links Between Problematic Smartphone Use and Grit Dimensions
authors: Luming Zhao, Jiaxi Peng
abstract: This study examined bidirectional longitudinal associations between grit dimensions (consistency of interest [CI] and perseverance of effort [PE]) and problematic smartphone use (PSU) and tested cognitive flexibility as a mediating mechanism. A sample of 1,641 Chinese university students (55.2 percent female; Mage = 20.1 years) completed measures at two time points 6 months apart. A four-variable cross-lagged panel model revealed that CI and PSU negatively predicted each other over time, whereas PSU unidirectionally predicted decreased PE. Cognitive flexibility partially mediated the PSU-to-PE pathway (indirect effect = −0.004, 95 percent bootstrap CI [−0.010, −0.0001]). Competing models analysis confirmed this directionality: the forward mediation (PSU → cognitive flexibility → PE) was significant, whereas the reverse was not. These findings demonstrate that grit dimensions exhibit distinct longitudinal patterns with PSU and identify cognitive flexibility as a cognitive mechanism through which PSU specifically undermines effort persistence. Implications for dimensional approaches to grit and targeted interventions are discussed.

title: Public Self-Consciousness and Anticipatory Avatar Customization in Korean Metaverse Platform
authors: Upyong Hong, Hyenyeong Chung, Yunju Nam
abstract: This study examines how public self-consciousness influences anticipatory avatar customization in Korean metaverse platform environments. In Study 1, 50 Korean university students created avatars under four conditions using iFland: free creation, private context, public context, and actual-self representation. Study 2 involved 100 independent raters evaluating the public suitability of freely created avatars. Results revealed that 96 percent created avatars differing from their actual appearance. Counterintuitively, individuals with higher public self-consciousness and agreeableness were significantly less likely to modify avatars for public contexts ( p < 0.05). Study 2 confirmed that unmodified avatars were rated more suitable for public contexts ( p < 0.05), suggesting that socially conscious individuals proactively incorporated appropriateness into initial designs. These preliminary findings suggest that Korean university students’ cultural emphasis on social harmony may shape virtual identity through anticipatory rather than reactive customization, though cross-cultural replication with diverse samples is needed to establish the generalizability of these patterns.

title: Online Social Anxiety in the Digital Age: Transitions, Predictors, and Mental Health Associations in Emerging Adulthood
authors: Ao Liu, Zheng Zhang, Xintian Hong, Rumiao Pan, Zhihao Ma, Yuanyuan Wang
abstract: Background: Online social anxiety (OSA), a multidimensional form of social evaluative anxiety in online social contexts, disproportionately affects emerging adults who constitute the largest active group of media users and face heightened psychological sensitivity due to growing pressures and immature sociocognitive regulation during the transition to adulthood. However, its heterogeneity, transitions, and longitudinal associations with mental health outcomes remain underexplored. Methods: This study utilized data from two waves of a three-wave longitudinal survey, with 849 Chinese participants ( Mean age = 21.6 years; 50.4 percent female) assessed at 4-month intervals. Individuals were classified using latent profile analysis and the stability and changes of profiles were assessed via latent transition analysis (LTA). Multinomial logistic regressions were conducted separately at baseline and follow-up to identify correlates of profile membership. Predictors of profile transitions were examined using manual three-step LTA models, and associations between latent transition patterns and follow-up mental health outcomes were examined using BCH-LTA distal outcome analyses controlling for the corresponding baseline symptom level. Results: Four profiles of OSA were identified: low, privacy-sensitive, moderate-high, and high OSA. Extreme profiles (low/high OSA) showed high stability (80.4 percent and 79.1 percent), while privacy-sensitive OSA exhibited the lowest stability (55.1 percent). Profile memberships were influenced by social-cognitive biases and digital interaction, particularly fear of negative evaluation and online interpersonal trust, whereas profile transitions were mainly associated with anxiety. Transitions toward less severe OSA profiles were generally associated with better subsequent mental health, whereas transitions toward more severe profiles corresponded to poorer outcomes, particularly for offline social anxiety. Conclusion: OSA was heterogeneous in its manifestation, severity and transitions. Personalized and early interventions targeting profile-specific vulnerabilities are critical to prevent the worsening of OSA and mitigate its psychological burden.

title: Trust beyond algorithms: What drives Italian audiences’ perceptions of search results and news produced with AI
authors: Giulia Sbaraini Fontes, Sergio Splendore
abstract: This article examines what drives audiences’ trust levels across different configurations of artificial intelligence (AI) use within the information ecosystem. We rely on a representative survey of Italian adults, performed in September 2025, to analyse trust patterns when (a) AI acts as an intermediary through automated search results and (b) when it is embedded in news organisations. Our findings show that AI-generated search results are more trusted than news, highlighting the growing role of platforms as primary information providers. Moreover, trust in news is positively associated with trust in news produced with AI, regardless of the source, challenging prevailing assumptions of ‘algorithmic aversion’ even in a traditional setting like Italy. These results suggest a shift in the foundations of media trust, with important implications for the role of journalism in an increasingly platform-driven information ecosystem.

title: Silent yet Not Deserted: Associations Between Ringer Modes, Mobile Phone Use, and Digital Stress
authors: Lise-Marie Nassen, Kathrin Karsay
abstract: While digital disconnection and smartphone regulation have gained scholarly attention, little is known about phone setting customizations. Currently, there is inconsistent evidence on whether modifying ringer modes reduces actual smartphone use and digital stress. Some studies suggest that a silent mode can reduce phone attentiveness, whereas others deem it ineffective or counterproductive. Drawing on self-determination theory, we explore the associations between preferred ringer mode, smartphone use (i.e., screen time and number of unlocks), and digital stress, alongside intrinsic and extrinsic motivations. We analyzed data from a quota-based survey of 386 smartphone users in Flanders (Belgium) using structural equation modeling multigroup analyses. Our study revealed few direct associations between preferred ringer mode and smartphone use or digital stress. However, our findings underscore the crucial role of motivation in choosing a ringer mode, revealing multiple significant associations among intrinsic and extrinsic motivations, phone use, and digital stress. We discuss these theoretical and empirical findings in light of self-determination theory.

title: Discourse competition and fragmented echoes: A computational frame analysis of climate change debate on Platform X
authors: Hao Gao, Yi Zheng, Ziqing Yang
abstract: Climate change communication is often framed as a contest between scientific knowledge and skepticism, but this binary overlooks fragmentation within the broader climate-concerned public. Drawing on cultural cognition theory, this study examines how competing discourse frames organize climate change debate on Twitter/X. A total of 556,470 English-language tweets posted between July 2014 and April 2024 were analyzed using Latent Dirichlet Allocation and Analysis of Topic Model Networks, supplemented with manual validation. The analysis identifies six discourse frames, dominated by Action & Responsibility, Political Process & Policy, Scientific Evidence & Impact, and Skepticism & Counter-Narrative. The findings show that skepticism consitutes a cohesive but minority discourse, while substantial fragmentation also separates scientific, activist, and policy-oriented communication. Scientific evidence remains weakly integrated into both mobilizational and institutional discourse, and grassroots activism is structurally separated from policy discussion. These patterns recast climate communication as a problem of coordination and cultural translation across “discourse islands,” rather than simply one of correcting misinformation or increasing the supply of scientific facts.

title: Make Campaigns Dance Again: The Trumpdance and the Memeaesthetic Logic of TikTok
authors: Cristopher Cepernich, Alice Fubini, Antonio Martella
abstract: TikTok’s mimesis-oriented affordances invite users to ‘perform’ politics through embodied, replicable templates. This article examines the Trumpdance – Donald Trump’s recurrent YMCA dance at campaign rallies – as a case of how offline events become a platform-native trend. Using the TikTok Research API, we collected 6799 Trumpdance-related videos posted during the final month of the 2024 U.S. presidential campaign. We extracted a stratified sample of the top 20% most-viewed videos per day and content-analyzed 1130 posts. Through Multiple Correspondence Analysis and hierarchical clustering, we identified six participation modes and modeled views and comments with negative binomial regression. Findings show that TikTok visibility concentrates on event-based remediation: clips of Trump dancing at rallies generate the highest expected views and comments, while supporter reenactments and playful appropriations circulate more narrowly. Discursive reframing and satirical remediation attract comparatively fewer views but can elicit intensive commenting, underscoring a split between algorithmic visibility and conversational engagement. We argue that ‘imitation publics’ support meaning-making and production but do not automatically translate into algorithmic visibility. Overall, the Trumpdance exemplifies what we label memeaesthetic: a communicative logic in which political performance becomes a shared aesthetic template for production and participation on TikTok.

title: Unpacking the Relationship Between Algorithmic Literacy and Misinformation: A Multidimensional Approach Using Two Sequential Studies
authors: Teresa Correa, Sebastián Valenzuela, Ingrid Bachmann, Nicolás Tobar Jorquera, Natalia Solís-Valdés, Isabel Pavez
abstract: Digital literacy is often proposed as a remedy for misinformation, yet empirical evidence regarding its effectiveness remains mixed. One reason for these inconsistencies lies in the multidimensional nature of both literacy and misinformation. This article focuses on algorithmic literacy, a distinct and increasingly central form of digital literacy in platform-mediated communication, and examines how its cognitive and behavioral dimensions relate to multiple facets of misinformation engagement. Drawing on two probabilistic survey studies conducted in Chile—a nationally representative face-to-face survey ( N = 1,200) and a random-digit-dial telephone survey of urban adults ( N = 2,265)—we analyze how cognitive (algorithmic awareness and knowledge) and behavioral (strategic actions to navigate algorithmic systems) dimensions of algorithmic literacy relate to perceived misinformation exposure, misinformation sharing, objective and subjective news knowledge, and knowledge miscalibration. Across both studies, a consistent pattern emerges: algorithmic literacy is more strongly associated with cognitive outcomes—especially perceived misinformation exposure and knowledge—than with behavioral outcomes like sharing. Higher algorithmic awareness consistently predicts greater perceived exposure, suggesting heightened recognition, while its link to sharing behavior is less consistent. These studies highlight the relevance of distinguishing cognitive from behavioral dimensions of literacy across different stages of misinformation engagement.

title: Anti-Elitism Gets the Views: Populist Communication and Popularity on German Political YouTube
authors: Lukas Erhard
abstract: YouTube has become a central venue for political communication, but systematic evidence of how parties employ the platform remains limited. This article examines how German political parties use YouTube and how populist rhetoric shapes engagement. We distinguish between anti-elitism and people-centrism and analyze their prevalence in party videos alongside their effects on video performance. We compile a dataset of official YouTube channels from all major German parties (2017–2025), apply automated transcription, and use a transformer-based model (PopBERT) to detect populist language. Video performance is assessed primarily through views, modeled with quantile regression and hurdle approaches to capture the likelihood of videos reaching the top tier and conditional effects among successful content. Our results show that the Alternative for Germany (AfD) far surpasses other parties in subscribers, video production, and engagement. Content analysis reveals that AfD channels contain markedly higher levels of anti-elitist rhetoric, while people-centrism appears more evenly distributed across the party spectrum. Quantile regression models show that anti-elitism is positively associated with engagement in the upper tail of the view distribution for all parties except the Free Democratic Party (FDP). Hurdle models further indicate that anti-elitism is associated with a higher probability of entering the top performance tier not only for the AfD but also for the Christian Democratic Union / Christian Social Union (CDU/CSU), Left, and the Social Democratic Party (SPD). Results for people-centrism are weaker and less consistent. The study contributes to research on digital populism by showing that anti-elitist rhetoric, more than people-centrism, is associated with video success on YouTube across populist and nonpopulist parties.

title: Online gendered violence and visibility in electoral autocracies: Evidence from multi-level elections in Türkiye
authors: Jungmin Han, Müge Finkel, Steven Finkel, Firat Duruşan, Erdem Yörük
abstract: Online platforms have become indispensable tools for political candidates to gain visibility, particularly for female candidates in electoral autocracies who often lack access to traditional networks, party hierarchies, and media platforms. We argue that online visibility, while a resource for female candidates, disproportionately exposes them to online violence that functions as a mechanism of political control, reinforcing patriarchal exclusion from the political sphere. Our analysis draws on more than three million tweets directed at 1,834 candidates across the 2023 parliamentary and 2024 local election campaigns in Türkiye, providing a rare opportunity to observe how these dynamics unfold at both the national and subnational levels. We find that while online visibility increases abuse for all candidates, the effect is markedly stronger for female candidates, who are disproportionately targeted across diverse forms of violence, including profanity, demeaning and ridiculing language, physical threats, and ethnic and religious hate speech. Moreover, our results suggest that in local elections, where candidates rely more heavily on personalized campaigns, increases in visibility are more strongly associated with female candidates’ exposure to online violence.

title: Debriefings in misinformation research should include fact-checks to correct misperceptions and increase perceived learning
authors: Emma Hoes, Sacha Altay
abstract: Debriefings are a cornerstone of ethical research, especially when deception is used. In misinformation experiments, debriefings both disclose the deception and warn participants about misinformation. Unlike other misinformation interventions, they reveal that researchers deliberately introduced the falsehoods, raising concerns about trust and skepticism. In a preregistered U.S. experiment (N = 896), we compare no debriefing, a general debriefing, and a specific debriefing with fact-checks and source links. Only the specific debriefing reduced belief in false claims participants saw, not in novel ones. The general debriefing slightly reduced belief in true news, suggesting warnings may heighten skepticism. Both improved attitudes toward the study and perceived transparency, supporting the use of specific debriefings as an ethical and effective practice in misinformation research.

title: Youth Nonresponse in Panel Surveys: Investigating the Impact of Life Events
authors: Camilla Salvatore, Peter Lugtig, Bella Struminskaya
abstract: Nonresponse in surveys is particularly problematic among young people in both cross-sectional and panel studies. This article investigates the factors driving lower participation rates among young people in longitudinal surveys. We study whether nonresponse can be explained by young people experiencing more life events associated with disengagement from panel surveys. Using data from the Understanding Society panel in the United Kingdom, we employ a discrete-time multinomial logistic hazard model to study nonresponse across panel waves. Consistent with previous research, our analysis identifies lower education, unemployment, immigrant background, and residential circumstances as key predictors of nonresponse. Furthermore, we demonstrate that changes in employment status and (expectations of) residential relocation significantly contribute to predicting attrition among young participants, with age remaining a significant factor. Living with parents also plays an important role, as it is associated with a lower risk of non-contact.
journal_full: Journal of Survey Statistics and Methodology

title: Varying the Content of Political Science Surveys to Improve the Survey Experience and Data Quality of Politically Disengaged Respondents
authors: Saskia Bartholomäus, Tobias Gummer
abstract: Respondents’ survey experience affects their answering and participation behavior and, consequently, measurement and nonresponse errors. Political science surveys especially suffer from biased estimates of political attitudes and behavior. Improving respondents’ survey experience by offering a more interesting and varied questionnaire poses a possible solution to this problem. In this regard, we break new ground by investigating whether improving politically disengaged respondents’ survey experience by including non-political survey content enhances data quality with respect to measurement and nonresponse errors in political science surveys. For this purpose, we conducted two survey experiments in a probability- and a nonprobability-based panel that varied the content of a political science questionnaire. This study provides the first evidence that offering a varied questionnaire rather than a purely political one lowered or even diminished the gap in measurement and nonresponse errors between politically engaged and disengaged respondents.
journal_full: Journal of Survey Statistics and Methodology
